verses.text: Do not envy wicked men or desire their company;
for their hearts devise violence, and their lips declare trouble.
By wisdom a house is built and by understanding it is established;
through knowledge its rooms are filled with every precious and beautiful treasure.
A wise man is strong, and a man of knowledge enhances his strength.
Only with sound guidance should you wage war, and victory lies in a multitude of counselors.
Wisdom is too high for a fool; he does not open his mouth in the meeting place.
He who plots evil will be called a schemer.
A foolish scheme is sin, and a mocker is detestable to men.
If you faint in the day of distress, how small is your strength!
Rescue those being led away to death, and restrain those stumbling toward the slaughter.
If you say, "Behold, we did not know about this," does not He who weighs hearts consider it? Does not the One who guards your life know? Will He not repay a man according to his deeds?
Eat honey, my son, for it is good, and the honeycomb is sweet to your taste.
Know therefore that wisdom is sweet to your soul. If you find it, there is a future for you, and your hope will never be cut off.
Do not lie in wait, O wicked man, near the dwelling of the righteous; do not destroy his resting place.
For though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up; but the wicked stumble in bad times.
Do not gloat when your enemy falls, and do not let your heart rejoice when he stumbles,
or the LORD will see and disapprove, and turn His wrath away from him.
Do not fret over evildoers, and do not be envious of the wicked.
For the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished.
My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not associate with the rebellious.
For they will bring sudden destruction. Who knows what ruin they can bring?
These also are sayings of the wise: To show partiality in judgment is not good.
Whoever tells the guilty, "You are innocent"— peoples will curse him, and nations will denounce him;
but it will go well with those who convict the guilty, and rich blessing will come upon them.
An honest answer given is like a kiss on the lips.
Complete your outdoor work and prepare your field; after that, you may build your house.
Do not testify against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips.
Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work."
I went past the field of a slacker and by the vineyard of a man lacking judgment.
Thorns had grown up everywhere, thistles had covered the ground, and the stone wall was broken down.
I observed and took it to heart; I looked and received instruction:
A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,
and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit.

context.author: “The wise,” whose words began at 22:17 and end at 24:22. A short appendix follows: “These also are sayings of the wise” (v.23).
context.genre: Wisdom sayings: short instructions, mostly two to four lines
context.audience: A son or student being trained (“my son”), perhaps for service at court (22:29; 23:1)
context.setting: “By wisdom a house is built and by understanding it is established” (v.3). The sayings call for courage: “If you faint in the day of distress, how small is your strength!” (v.10). “Rescue those being led away to death” (v.11), and do not pretend you did not know, for He who weighs hearts sees (v.12). “Though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up” (v.16), but do not gloat when your enemy falls (v.17). A second, shorter collection begins at v.23 with a warning against partiality in judgment, a note that an honest answer is like a kiss (v.26), and a ban on revenge (v.29). The chapter ends with the teacher’s story of passing a slacker’s vineyard, overgrown with thorns and its stone wall broken down (vv.30-34).
context.custom: Vineyards were walled with stone to keep out animals, and a wall left unrepaired soon fell (v.31). Thorns and nettles took over untended ground quickly. Fearing the king alongside the LORD (v.21) reflected the belief that God gave the king his rule (Romans 13:1-7; 1 Peter 2:17).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 25 begins a new collection: proverbs of Solomon copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah.
context.timelineBible: Verses 33-34 repeat 6:10-11 almost exactly. Verse 12 is echoed in Romans 2:6 and Matthew 16:27: God “will repay each one according to his deeds” (Romans 2:6). Jesus’ “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44) goes beyond v.17.

translation.meaning: Trouble, a tight place. The word sounds like the word for “small” (tsar) in the same verse.
To weigh, measure, test. God weighs hearts.
A vineyard, usually walled, with a watchtower and a winepress.

gospelParallels.note: God will repay each one according to his deeds (v.12).
Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.

otBackground.note: A little sleep, a little slumber.
The song of the vineyard whose wall is broken.
Though I have fallen, I will rise.

overview.summary: Wisdom builds a house; rescue the perishing, get up when you fall, do not gloat or take revenge, and learn from the slacker’s ruined vineyard.
overview.settingLine: The wise teacher walks past a ruined vineyard.

history.t: The words of the wise, then more sayings.
Judges were not to show favor.

customs.t: Judgment was given at the gate.

archaeology.t: Stone terraces and field walls still cover the hills of Judah.
Round stone field towers guarded vineyards at harvest.

overview.discussion: “Though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up” (v.16). What helps me get back up when I fall?
overview.book: The book of Proverbs · 31 chapters. Short sayings and longer poems that teach how to live wisely in God’s world, beginning with the fear of the LORD.
overview.author: “The wise” (22:17)
